lead: A rigid body does not bend or stretch, so a force can slide along its line of action, and a force at one point can be replaced by the same force at another point plus a couple. This unit turns that idea into working tools: moments, couples, reduction of force systems, support reactions, equilibrium equations and virtual work. After it you can take a loaded bracket, beam or lever, draw its free body diagram, find the reactions at its supports, and check the answer by a second method.
about: This unit treats the body as rigid: only the magnitude, direction and line of action of a force matter. Chapter 2.1 gives transmissibility, the rule that lets a force slide along its line of action. Chapter 2.2 defines the moment of a force about a point and about an axis, and 2.3 adds component moments by Varignon's theorem. Chapter 2.4 builds couples, and 2.5 reduces any force system to a resultant plus a couple. Chapter 2.6 lists supports and their reactions, and 2.7 writes the equilibrium equations in two and three dimensions. Chapter 2.8 uses two-force and three-force bodies as shortcuts, and 2.9 solves equilibrium problems by virtual work instead of force equations.

chapters.idea: A force acting on a rigid body may be moved anywhere along its line of action without changing the external effect on the body.
chapters.depth: Statement of the principle, the line of action, and the difference between rigid and deformable bodies. Forces on a rigid body are sliding vectors: only magnitude, direction and line of action count. Two consequences: a force may be slid to a joint or corner, and it may be slid to a common point before forces are added. Say that internal forces change even when external effects do not. Some syllabi call it the principle of transmissibility of forces.

figure.title: Sliding a force on a rigid body
figure.aria: A force of 100 N applied at point A slides along its line of action to point B, and the reactions of the rigid body stay the same.

chapters.example: A rigid plate is pinned at O. A force of 100 N acts at a point A on the plate, and its line of action passes 0.4 m from O. The force is then moved to a point B further along the same line of action, 1.2 m from O measured along that line. Find the moment about O in both positions. Perpendicular distance from O to the line of action is still 0.4 m, so M_O = 100 N × 0.4 m = 40 N·m in both cases. The pin reactions are unchanged too, but the internal force inside the plate is not.
chapters.trap: Sliding a force changes the internal forces, so the principle fails for a deformable body such as a rope, or a truss member you are checking for stress. It never allows turning the force or changing its magnitude.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: force as a vector, resolution of forces.
chapters.leave: Internal forces and stresses; the reduction of many forces to chapter 2.5.

chapters.idea: The moment of a force about a point measures its turning effect, and the moment about an axis is the part of that turning effect along the axis.
chapters.depth: M_O = r × F as a vector and M = F d as a scalar, where d is the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action. Units N·m. Sign convention: anticlockwise positive in a plane, right-hand rule in space. Moment about an axis through A and B: M_AB = u · (r × F), the scalar triple product written as a 3×3 determinant, with u the unit vector along the axis. Two zero cases: the force is parallel to the axis, or the force cuts the axis. Some syllabi call the axis case the moment of a force about a line.

figure.aria: A position vector r runs from the moment centre O to the point A where force F acts, and a separate dashed line PQ marks the axis about which the moment is taken.

chapters.example: A force F = 3i + 4j − 2k N acts at the point A(1, 2, 3) m. Find its moment about the origin O, and about the x-axis. r = 1i + 2j + 3k m. M_O = r × F gives M_x = y F_z − z F_y = 2(−2) − 3(4) = −16 N·m, M_y = z F_x − x F_z = 3(3) − 1(−2) = 11 N·m, M_z = x F_y − y F_x = 1(4) − 2(3) = −2 N·m. So M_O = −16i + 11j − 2k N·m. The moment about the x-axis is the i component, −16 N·m, meaning 16 N·m clockwise looking along +x.
chapters.trap: Order in the cross product: M_O = r × F with r drawn from the moment point to the point of application. Writing F × r flips the sign. For an axis, forgetting that u must be a unit vector.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: vector algebra, cross product; chapter 2.1 for the line of action.
chapters.leave: Varignon's theorem to 2.3, couples to 2.4, reduction of a full system to 2.5.

chapters.idea: The moment of a force about a point equals the sum of the moments of its components about the same point.
chapters.depth: Statement for any number of components, with the components acting at the same point of application. Proof in a plane by writing F_x and F_y and using M = x F_y − y F_x. Use it for inclined forces, where perpendicular distances are awkward, and to replace one force by two convenient ones. Extend to an axis: add the moments of the components about the axis. State clearly when the theorem does not apply: components placed at a different point along the line of action are still fine, but different lines are not.

figure.aria: The total moment M_O of one force is shown splitting into three component moments F₁d₁, F₂d₂ and F₃d₃ that add up to it.

chapters.example: A force of 50 N acts at a point A that is 3 m to the right and 1 m above O. The force points up and to the right at 30° to the horizontal. Find its moment about O. Components at A: F_x = 50 cos30 = 43.3 N, F_y = 50 sin30 = 25 N. Then M_O = x F_y − y F_x = 3(25) − 1(43.3) = 75 − 43.3 = 31.7 N·m anticlockwise. Check by the perpendicular distance: d = 31.7/50 = 0.634 m, which is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action.
chapters.trap: Using the slant distance in place of the perpendicular distance, and losing signs when one component turns the body the other way. Both components must act at the same point of application.
chapters.leave: Position of the resultant to 2.5; centroid of a distributed load to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces form a couple, and a couple has the same moment about every point in space.
chapters.depth: Definition of a couple, with couple moment M = F d, where d is the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action; direction by the right-hand rule; units N·m. The couple moment is a free vector: it is the same about every point and may be drawn anywhere on the body. Equivalent couples have the same M. Couples add as vectors. Replace a force at A by the same force at O plus a couple M = F d; some syllabi call this translation of a force to a parallel position, and the pair is a force-couple system. Moment of a couple about a line is the projection of M on the unit vector of the line.

figure.aria: A force at A is shifted to the point O by adding a cancelling pair F and −F at O, which leaves the force at O plus a couple of moment F times d.

chapters.example: A force of 120 N acts vertically downward at the point A(0.6, 0) m on a plate. Replace it by an equivalent force-couple system at the origin O. F = −120j N at r = 0.6i m. M_O = x F_y − y F_x = 0.6(−120) − 0 = −72 N·m, that is 72 N·m clockwise. The equivalent system is a 120 N force down at O plus a clockwise couple of 72 N·m. Because a couple is a free vector, that 72 N·m is the same about any point of the plate.
chapters.trap: Believing the couple moment depends on the reference point; it does not. Using the distance between the two points of application instead of the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action.
chapters.leave: Reduction of many forces at once to 2.5.

chapters.idea: Any system of forces can be replaced by one resultant force at a chosen point plus one couple, and often by a single force alone.
chapters.depth: Equivalence: two systems are equivalent when they give the same ΣF and the same ΣM about one point, and then about every point. Reduction at O: R = ΣF and M_O = Σ M_O from all the forces. If R·M_O = 0 and R ≠ 0, the pair becomes a single force at the perpendicular offset d = M_O/R. Special cases: R = 0 with M_O ≠ 0 gives a pure couple; R ≠ 0 with R parallel to M_O gives a wrench; both zero is equilibrium. For coplanar non-concurrent forces, find magnitude, direction and the line of action by Varignon. Distributed loads: resultant equals the area under the load diagram and acts at its centroid (cross-reference Unit 4).

figure.aria: A general force system is reduced to a resultant R and a moment M about a point O; if R dot M is zero the pair collapses to a single force shifted by d, otherwise a wrench or a couple remains.

chapters.example: Three coplanar forces act on a plate: F₁ = 10 N along +y at A(0, 0), F₂ = 20 N along +x at B(0, 2) m, F₃ = 15 N along −y at C(4, 0) m. Find the resultant and where its line of action cuts the x-axis. R = (0 + 20 + 0)i + (10 + 0 − 15)j = 20i − 5j N, so |R| = 20.6 N at 14.0° below the +x axis. M_O = Σ(x F_y − y F_x) = 0 + [0(0) − 2(20)] + [4(−15) − 0] = −40 − 60 = −100 N·m. On the x-axis, y = 0, so x R_y = −100 gives x(−5) = −100 and x = 20 m. The resultant is a 20.6 N force cutting the x-axis at 20 m from O, turning the plate clockwise.
chapters.trap: Summing moments about different points for different forces. Also, R = 0 does not mean equilibrium when M_O ≠ 0; a pure couple is left over.
chapters.leave: Centroids of areas and distributed loads to Unit 4; support reactions to 2.6.

chapters.idea: Each kind of support removes certain motions and, in return, supplies a fixed number of reaction components.
chapters.depth: Name and draw: roller or rocker, one reaction normal to the surface; smooth surface contact, one reaction normal; short link or cable, one reaction along it; pin or hinge, two reactions F_x and F_y; slider or guide; fixed support, three reactions F_x, F_y and M; in space, ball-and-socket gives three forces and a fixed base gives three forces and three moments. Count unknowns: more than three unknown reactions in a plane problem makes it statically indeterminate. Say that the assumed direction is free, and a negative answer simply reverses it.

figure.aria: A stack of supports from most to least restraint: fixed support with three reactions, pin with two, roller with one normal reaction.

chapters.example: A vertical pole 3 m tall is fixed to the ground at A. A horizontal force of 200 N to the right and a vertical load of 500 N downward both act at the free top end B. Find the reactions at A. ΣF_x = 0 gives A_x = −200 N, that is 200 N to the left. ΣF_y = 0 gives A_y = 500 N upward. Take moments about A: the horizontal force at height 3 m gives 3(200) = 600 N·m clockwise, and the vertical load gives no moment because its line passes through A. So the fixed support supplies M_A = 600 N·m anticlockwise.
chapters.trap: Giving a pin a moment reaction, or a roller two reactions. On an inclined surface the roller reaction is perpendicular to the surface, not vertical.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2; free body diagram from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: Friction at a rough support to Unit 3; supports of trusses and frames to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A rigid body is in equilibrium when the sum of all forces and the sum of all moments about any point are both zero.
chapters.depth: ΣF = 0 and ΣM_O = 0 about any point O. In a plane this gives three scalar equations, ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣM_O = 0, so three unknown reactions at most. Other valid sets: two moment equations about different points plus one force equation, or three moment equations about three non-collinear points. In space, six equations, ΣF_x, ΣF_y, ΣF_z and ΣM_x, ΣM_y, ΣM_z, so six unknowns at most. Method: free body diagram, choose axes, choose a moment point that removes unknowns, solve, check with an unused equation.

figure.aria: The equilibrium recipe: draw the free body diagram, write the two force equations and one moment equation in a plane, solve for the reactions and check that the unknowns never exceed three.

chapters.example: A massless beam AB of length 3 m is hinged to a wall at A and held by a cable at B. The cable makes 45° with the beam and pulls up and toward the wall. A load of 500 N hangs from the beam at 2 m from A. Find the cable tension and the hinge reaction. Take moments about A: the tension at B has a vertical component T sin45 at 3 m, so 3(0.7071T) − 2(500) = 0, giving T = 471 N. ΣF_x = 0 gives A_x = 0.7071(471) = 333 N away from the wall. ΣF_y = 0 gives A_y = 500 − 333 = 167 N upward.
chapters.trap: A horizontal force applied above the moment point still has a moment; students often drop it. Forgetting the self-weight, or taking moments about a point that leaves two unknowns in the same equation.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.2 and 2.6; equilibrium of a particle from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: Trusses, frames and friction to Unit 3; the equilibrium of a body that also moves to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A body loaded at only two points has its two forces collinear, and a body loaded with three coplanar forces in equilibrium has them concurrent or parallel.
chapters.depth: Two-force body: forces at two points only, no applied couple, weight neglected; the two forces are equal, opposite and act along the line joining the points, so the member is in tension or compression. Three-force body: three coplanar forces in equilibrium must have concurrent lines of action, or all parallel; the proof takes moments about the point where two of them meet. Use it to find the direction of a hinge reaction without solving the full equation set. Only a few syllabi use the name three-force member.

figure.aria: Three forces acting at points A, B and C all have lines of action that pass through the single point O.

chapters.example: A uniform rod AB of length 2 m and weight 300 N is hinged to a vertical wall at A and held by a horizontal string at B. The rod makes 30° with the wall. Find the string tension and the hinge reaction. Three forces act: the weight down through the midpoint, the tension horizontal at B, and the hinge reaction at A. The weight line is at x = 1 sin30 = 0.5 m and the tension line is at y = 2 cos30 = 1.732 m, so the three lines meet at (0.5, 1.732) m. Moments about A: T(1.732) = 300(0.5), so T = 86.6 N. Then R_x = 86.6 N and R_y = 300 N, giving a hinge reaction of 312 N at 16.1° from the wall.
chapters.trap: Calling a member two-force when it carries its own weight, a couple, or a load at a third point. Three forces are concurrent only if they are coplanar and no couple acts.
chapters.leave: Tension and compression in truss members to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A system in equilibrium does zero total virtual work for every small displacement that the supports allow.
chapters.depth: Virtual displacement: imaginary, infinitesimal, consistent with the supports, with time frozen. Virtual work of a force δU = F · δr = F δr cos θ. Ideal reactions, such as a smooth pin, a roller, a rigid link or a cable, do no work. Principle: a system in equilibrium satisfies δU = 0 for every virtual displacement. Method: pick one coordinate θ, write the position of each load as x(θ) and y(θ), differentiate to get δx and δy, add the work of the active forces, set the sum to zero. Use it for linkages, ladders and connected beams, where the force equations would need several unknown reactions. Only a few syllabi go on to Lagrange's equations.

figure.aria: The virtual work method: choose one angle, write the positions of the loads in terms of it, set the total virtual work to zero, and solve for the unknown force.

chapters.example: A uniform rod AB of length 2 m and weight 200 N is hinged to a vertical wall at A and held by a horizontal force P applied at B. The rod makes 30° with the wall. Find P by virtual work. With θ measured from the wall, x_B = 2 sinθ and the height of the centre of gravity is y_G = 1 cosθ. So δx_B = 2 cosθ δθ and δy_G = −sinθ δθ. The weight does work (−200)(δy_G) = 200 sinθ δθ, and P does work P δx_B. Setting the sum to zero: 2P cosθ + 200 sinθ = 0, so P = −100 tanθ = −57.7 N. The minus sign means P must act toward the wall, with magnitude 57.7 N.
chapters.trap: Giving work to reaction forces at ideal supports, and using a real displacement instead of a virtual one. Differentiate the position correctly: δx = (dx/dθ) δθ.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.7; dot product from Unit 1; basic differentiation from mathematics.
chapters.leave: Lagrange's equations, stability and energy methods for moving bodies to later courses and to Unit 6.
